name: The Holy Family of Jesus, Mary, and Joseph
briefBio: The feast honors Jesus, Mary, and Joseph together. Matthew narrates a house in Bethlehem, danger under Herod, flight to Egypt, return, and settlement in Nazareth; Luke gives a distinct birth, presentation, Jewish-law observance, Nazareth return, and Temple episode. These accounts should not be silently harmonized into a complete domestic diary. Mark later shows Jesus widening kinship around doing God's will. The feast spread universally through a 1921 decree and now falls on the Sunday within Christmas's octave, or December 30 when no Sunday occurs. Social history makes household reconstruction hypothetical and warns against projecting modern or elite models; evidence does not establish the family's exact wealth. The flight supports solidarity with displaced people without equating ancient narrative and modern legal categories. Q618057 fits the biblical family group, but shared lifespan, age, and vocation are omitted. This white feast cannot enforce rigid roles, unsafe obedience, domestic coercion, fertility pressure, anti-LGBTQ stigma, poverty romanticism, or anti-migrant exclusion.
feastDates: Sunday within the Octave of Christmas, or December 30 if no Sunday occurs

sources.title: Matthew, Chapter 2
sources.authorOrInstitution: United States Conference of Catholic Bishops
sources.reuseBasis: Canonical Scripture used with narrative attribution for Jesus, Mary, and Joseph in a Bethlehem house, threat, flight to Egypt, return, and settlement at Nazareth; it is not a complete domestic biography or exact analogue for every modern migration status

sources.title: Luke, Chapter 2
sources.authorOrInstitution: United States Conference of Catholic Bishops
sources.reuseBasis: Canonical Scripture used for Luke's distinct birth, presentation, Jewish-law observance, return to Nazareth, growth summary, and Temple episode; differences from Matthew are preserved and child obedience is never read to override safeguarding

sources.title: Mark, Chapter 3
sources.authorOrInstitution: United States Conference of Catholic Bishops
sources.reuseBasis: Canonical Scripture used for tension around Jesus's family and his widening of kinship toward those doing God's will; biological or nuclear household form is not made an absolute measure of Christian belonging

sources.title: Nonnulla Festa cum Officiis et Missis Propriis ad Universam Ecclesiam Extenduntur
sources.publisher: Acta Apostolicae Sedis 13 (1921), pp. 543–544; The Holy See
sources.reuseBasis: Official decree of 26 October 1921 used at AAS pp. 543–544 for universal extension of the Holy Family feast, then assigned to the Sunday within the Epiphany octave, with domestic devotional rationale and effect from 1922; current placement comes from the separate calendar

sources.title: Marialis Cultus, no. 5
sources.reuseBasis: Formal liturgical reception used for the Feast of the Holy Family within the renewed Christmas season and contemplation of the holy life of Jesus, Mary, and Joseph; it is not independent social history or a universal household-role template

sources.title: La familia en la Galilea del siglo primero
sources.publisher: Estudios Bíblicos 53(4) (1995), pp. 461–488; Universidad Eclesiástica San Dámaso repository
sources.reuseBasis: Repository record and indexed full-text content used especially at pp. 486–488 for the hypothetical character of reconstructing first-century Galilean family life, varied household realities, and warnings against projecting modern or elite models; it does not establish a detailed Holy Family household biography

sources.title: Poverty in the first-century Galilee
sources.publisher: HTS Teologiese Studies/Theological Studies 72(4) (2016), article a3398; DOI 10.4102/hts.v72i4.3398; CC BY
sources.reuseBasis: Full peer-reviewed article used for widespread Galilean precarity, taxation, labor, and scholarly disagreement over Jesus's family's social position; regional poverty evidence does not prove the Holy Family's exact wealth or license romanticized deprivation

sources.title: Amoris Laetitia
sources.reuseBasis: Formal pastoral teaching used especially at nos. 32, 49, 53–57, 197–198, 241, and 246 for varied and extended family realities, single parents, migrants, disability, poverty, violence and abuse, children's protection, and accompaniment; it is a safeguard source, not archival Holy Family biography

sources.title: Message for the 93rd World Day of Migrants and Refugees: The Migrant Family
sources.reuseBasis: Readable official English message used for ecclesial reception of Matthew's Holy Family in Egypt alongside modern migrant and refugee families, their hardship, dignity, welcome, and integration; analogy motivates solidarity but does not establish identical legal categories or guarantee protection

sources.authorOrInstitution: Liturgy Office, Catholic Bishops' Conference of England and Wales
sources.publisher: Catholic Bishops' Conference of England and Wales
sources.reuseBasis: Formal universal calendar used for the Holy Family feast on the Sunday within the octave of the Lord's Birth or December 30 if no Sunday occurs; it does not establish biography or color

sources.authorOrInstitution: United States Conference of Catholic Bishops

editorial.reviewer: Catholic Daily factual and theological review

whyItMatters: The Holy Family places incarnation inside kinship, danger, worship, work, growth, and migration while resisting a single household template. Their feast calls every family and community toward safety, mutual care, truthful dialogue, welcome, and belonging beyond blood alone.
oneMinuteSummary: The feast honors Jesus, Mary, and Joseph together. Matthew narrates Bethlehem, danger, flight to Egypt, return, and settlement in Nazareth. Luke offers a distinct birth, presentation, Jewish-law observance, Nazareth return, growth, and Temple story. These accounts are not a complete domestic diary and should not be silently harmonized. Mark also widens kinship beyond blood toward doing God's will. The feast was extended universally in 1921 and now falls on Sunday within Christmas's octave, or December 30 when no Sunday occurs; its color is white. Social history makes reconstruction of Galilean households hypothetical and does not establish this family's exact wealth. Their flight supports solidarity with displaced families without collapsing ancient narrative into modern legal status. The Holy Family cannot enforce rigid gender roles, domestic coercion, unsafe child obedience, anti-LGBTQ stigma, fertility pressure, nuclear-family superiority, poverty romanticism, anti-migrant exclusion, or promises of prosperity and protection.

sections.heading: Two infancy narratives, not one diary
sections.body: Matthew and Luke identify Jesus, Mary, Joseph, Bethlehem, and Nazareth but arrange distinct journeys and theological emphases. Matthew includes flight and return; Luke includes presentation and Temple. Faithful reading preserves each voice rather than inventing daily scenes or silently harmonizing every movement.

sections.heading: Jewish family, work, and social limits
sections.body: Luke explicitly locates the family within Jewish law and worship. Galilean social history illuminates households, labor, taxation, and precarity but remains hypothetical and varied. It cannot prove exact wealth, daily tasks, universal gender roles, or a romantic ideal of poverty.

sections.heading: Flight and solidarity without collapse
sections.body: Matthew portrays a family fleeing royal danger. Later Catholic reception connects that story with migrants and refugees and calls for welcome and dignity. The analogy invites solidarity, but ancient narrative and modern legal categories are not identical, and devotion guarantees no family's safety.

sections.heading: Feast, varied families, and safety
sections.body: The feast became universal in 1921 and later moved into Christmas's octave. Mark prevents nuclear-family absolutism, while pastoral teaching names single-parent and extended families, disability, poverty, migration, violence, abuse, and children's safety. Obedience never means remaining in harm or concealing abuse.

life.gospelTheme: The Word enters embodied family life and widens kinship into a community of truth, safety, welcome, mutual care, and doing God's will.
life.struggle: Families face danger, displacement, economic pressure, misunderstanding, and abuse; idealized religious models can intensify shame and coercive control.
life.response: Preserve each person's dignity, protect children and adults from harm, welcome displaced neighbors, share work, and honor varied households without stigma.

virtues.name: Protective responsiveness
virtues.evidence: Matthew portrays Joseph responding to danger by taking the child and Mary away and later reassessing where to settle.
virtues.imitation: Believe a credible safety concern, consult trained support, and help the affected person choose a safer next step without demanding secrecy or obedience.

virtues.name: Hospitable kinship
virtues.evidence: Mark widens family around doing God's will, while migration teaching receives the Holy Family as a call to welcome displaced families.
virtues.imitation: Offer one practical, consent-based welcome to a migrant, single-parent, adoptive, blended, extended, or chosen family without judging its conformity to your household.

practice.spiritual: Pray for your household and for people whose family life does not fit an idealized image, asking God for safety and belonging.
practice.action: Check one household practice for consent and safety, then support a migrant or varied family through a trusted local organization.

reflectionQuestions: Does my picture of holy family life make vulnerable people safer, or pressure them to hide harm and difference?
How can my household or community widen belonging without demanding sameness?

scripture.connection: Jesus widens kinship around doing God's will, preventing the Holy Family feast from becoming an absolute or exclusionary nuclear-household template.

prayer: God who dwelt among us in Jesus, bless every household seeking love and safety. Through Mary and Joseph teach us to protect without controlling, work without exploiting, welcome displaced neighbors, and widen belonging. Free families from violence, shame, and rigid roles. Amen.
